Title: Latency-robust corridor supervisory control for hybrid nuclear–HVDC–renewable power systems under communication-constrained low-inertia operation
Abstract: Hybrid nuclear–HVDC–renewable transmission corridors introduce new supervisory coordination challenges due to reduced inertia, heterogeneous asset dynamics, and non-negligible bounded communication delay. Conventional coordination approaches typically assume ideal communication or treat latency as a secondary implementation issue, limiting robustness under wide-area supervisory operation. This paper proposes Latency-Robust Corridor Supervisory Control (LR-CSC), a reproducible engineering framework for delay-robust supervisory coordination under bounded communication delay. The methodology integrates a compact corridor-level state-space representation, a delay-embedded min–max supervisory formulation, and a digital-twin-based feasibility screening engine. Rather than relying on continuous online optimisation or centralised control authority, LR-CSC evaluates candidate supervisory actions over an admissible state envelope and enforces constraint satisfaction for all delays within a specified design bound. Validation is conducted using a fully specified synthetic nuclear–HVDC–renewable corridor benchmark under disturbance variation, stochastic bounded communication delay, and inertia degradation. Results demonstrate three principal outcomes. First, embedding bounded communication delay directly within supervisory feasibility expands the stable inertia–delay operating region relative to delay-blind coordination strategies. Second, delay-embedded feasibility screening suppresses oscillatory interaction between fast converter dynamics and slower synchronous response, yielding improved frequency nadir, reduced peak RoCoF, and faster settling behaviour. Third, robustness improvements persist across Monte-Carlo disturbance and communication uncertainty scenarios, indicating that performance gains arise from structural delay-embedded supervisory coordination rather than scenario-specific tuning. The proposed framework is intentionally positioned as a supervisory feasibility layer for low-inertia corridor coordination and provides a transparent balance between bounded computation, reproducibility, and practical implementability under communication-constrained operation. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Qiu W.; Chen S.; Zhang J.
Title: Uncertainty-aware digital twins for safe operation and active fault-tolerance in degrading heterogeneous pumping systems
Abstract: Conventional deterministic controls often fail in fluid systems under mechanical degradation due to epistemic uncertainties, leading to constraint violations. While passive fault diagnosis has advanced, autonomous risk-averse decision-making post-degradation remains lacking. To bridge this gap, this study proposes an Adaptive Probabilistic Digital Twin (APDT) framework. Utilizing Uncertainty Quantification (UQ), the APDT establishes mathematical guardrails based on the Probability of Feasibility, actively preventing physical boundary violations under deep uncertainties. Furthermore, the framework dynamically reconstructs system mappings online to adapt to non-stationary asymmetrical degradation, overcoming the limitations of static models. An embedded Trust-Region mechanism ensures smooth state transitions by preventing actuator fatigue. Crucially, trajectory analysis reveals an emergent “strategic offloading” behavior: the APDT autonomously shifts operational loads from degraded to healthy units. This acts as an active fault-tolerant mechanism, mitigating stress on deteriorating components to prevent sudden failures while maintaining robust output. Ultimately, the APDT offers a reliable, physics-compliant paradigm for the active safety management and life-extension of cyber-physical systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Spatial–temporal event compiler: Look-around reasoning for uncertainty-aware synchronization in digital twin-driven manufacturing systems
Abstract: Personalized production is widely adopted in discrete manufacturing due to its ability to meet diverse customer requirements through flexible combinations of components. However, it also poses significant challenges to production synchronization, which requires all necessary operators, tools, materials, and industrial robots to be available within the prescribed time and space. In complex multi-stage manufacturing processes, execution deviations can accumulate into operation-level uncertainty, namely the risk that an operation cannot start, proceed, or finish as scheduled because the required resources and execution conditions are no longer aligned. Such uncertainty undermines resource utilization and may trigger cascading delays across the entire process. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a spatial–temporal event compiler (STEC) framework comprising digital, knowledge, and reasoning engines for compiling and analyzing manufacturing events. Specifically, the state information of digital models is compiled into a spatial–temporal event graph, which is continuously updated through a multi-clock alignment scheme that aligns distinct planning, scheduling, and execution time scales. Within the reasoning engine, a look-around reasoning approach is developed to capture historical consistency, the current execution context, and near-future evolution trends by integrating look-backward, look-present, and look-forward perspectives, thereby enabling uncertainty assessment. Furthermore, an LLM-based synchronization mechanism is incorporated into the framework to provide status reports through multi-turn interactions, allowing managers to query the current execution status and assess potential downstream impacts for timely intervention. Finally, a case study demonstrates that STEC improves the accuracy and stability of uncertainty identification. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Towards efficient parametric state estimation with shallow recurrent decoder networks: Application to circulating fuel reactors
Abstract: The recent developments in data-driven methods have paved the way for new methodologies to provide accurate and robust full state reconstruction of engineering systems under any operating conditions. Such approaches can be attractive for next-generation nuclear reactors, which represent particularly challenging applications for sensing and monitoring due to the complexity of the strongly coupled physics involved and the extremely harsh environments. Data-driven techniques can combine different sources of information, including computational proxy models and noisy measurements on the system, to robustly estimate the state. This work leverages the novel Shallow Recurrent Decoder (SHRED) architecture to infer the entire state vector (both neutronics and fluid dynamics fields) of a circulating fuel reactor, the Molten Salt Fast Reactor. The standard architecture is extended to treat parametric time-series data, ensuring the possibility of investigating different scenarios and showing its capabilities to provide an accurate state estimation in various conditions. The proposed methodology adopts possible innovative sensing strategies in new-generation reactors, including out-of-core time-series neutron flux measurements alone, in-core sensing measuring the precursor concentrations or mobile probes advected by the fuel flow. The promising results of this work are further strengthened by the possibility of quantifying the uncertainty associated with the state estimation due to the considerably low training cost of the architecture. The ability of SHRED to deliver real-time, system-wide reconstruction highlights its potential for reactor monitoring, control, and digital twin development in next-generation circulating fuel systems. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: A hybrid model calibration framework for transient seepage prediction in levees using field monitoring data
Abstract: Accurate prediction of transient pore-water pressure (PWP) is essential for reliable assessment of levee performance and decision-making, as seepage-driven processes directly influence failure mechanisms such as slope instability, uplift, and internal erosion. Physics-based numerical seepage models are widely used in engineering practice, but their predictive accuracy is often limited by model parameter uncertainty, simplified boundary conditions, and unmodeled processes, particularly under transient hydrologic forcing. These limitations introduce uncertainty in evaluating levee performance under extreme events. This study develops a hybrid modeling framework that enhances predictive accuracy while preserving the physical consistency of numerical seepage models. The framework integrates transient finite-element (FE) seepage modeling, sensitivity-guided parameter calibration, and a data-driven residual-learning layer based on a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. The LSTM is trained exclusively to learn structured residual errors between FE predictions and field measurements and operates as an additive correction without modifying governing equations. Application to a field-instrumented levee demonstrates that while calibration improves overall agreement, systematic discrepancies persist under transient conditions. The residual-learning layer reduces prediction error by approximately 70%, lowering the RMSE from about 11 cm to approximately 3. Interpretability analysis using TimeSHAP confirms that residual corrections are governed primarily by physically meaningful drivers, including hydrologic forcing and recent system state. By reducing structured model discrepancy, the proposed framework improves transient seepage predictions while retaining a physics-based predictive baseline and providing transparency into the factors governing residual correction. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future sensor-integrated digital-twin applications as additional validation data become available. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Trustworthy artificial intelligence in advanced manufacturing
Abstract: Additive manufacturing is relying more and more on artificial intelligence for prediction, control, and real-time decisions. Deployment, however, is still difficult. The main reason is that the underlying thermal, flow, and microstructural behavior can shift as the process changes, which makes reliable model performance hard to maintain. This review examines how trustworthy artificial intelligence (TAI) can be used to close that gap in digital twins for additive manufacturing across both metallic and ceramic systems. It frames trustworthiness as a technical condition for deployment and translates it into an AM-specific operational framework. From that point onward, it examines how current workflows handle reliability, uncertainty quantification, interpretability, explainability, robustness, generalizability, fairness, and transparency. A structured evaluation of sixty studies in metallic and ceramic additive manufacturing systems reveals a distinct trend. Robustness and generalizability receive much more attention than transparency, explainability, and fairness. The coverage is also stronger in metallic systems than in ceramic ones. To move beyond binary classification, the review further applies a structured evidence-depth rubric that distinguishes absent coverage, limited or implicit evidence, method-level evidence, and operational evidence for each TAI attribute. We further show that trustworthy deployment depends on more than predictive accuracy. It also depends on physically consistent models as well as updates that account for uncertainty. Decision support has to remain interpretable as well. Model transfer across machines and materials should be treated as controlled adaptation, where reusable physics, sensing, and validation elements are separated from material-specific features that require recalibration. The validation path must also support qualification and industrial deployment, leading to a more cohesive digital twin framework. It brings together physics-based models, reduced-order models, learning-based surrogates, multimodal sensing, and trust-aware evaluation. The main finding is that trustworthiness is the missing technical link between digital twins that can be confidently used in advanced manufacturing and promising AI-enabled demonstrations. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Prediction of cooking-induced food transformations: A survey and outlook towards machine learning
Abstract: Cooking induces coupled physical, chemical, and biological transformations that jointly determine food safety, nutritional value, and sensory quality. Predicting cooking-induced food transformations is therefore a central challenge, receiving growing attention across applications including process optimisation in the food industry, product design, quality control, personalised cooking, and the development of smart appliances and digital twins. Despite extensive progress in food process engineering, robust prediction across foods, geometries, and operating conditions remains difficult due to the multiscale heterogeneity of food matrices, substantial process variability, and experimental data that are often sparse, noisy, or destructive to acquire. To stimulate future research, this survey provides a comprehensive review of modelling approaches for cooking-induced transformations and articulates a structured outlook towards machine learning (ML). We first consolidate the scientific background on food cooking processes. We then introduce a principled taxonomy of conventional models and analyse how their encoded structure can act as inductive bias for data-driven learning. Building on this foundation, we formalise cooking prediction as learning mappings from initial product state and process descriptors to time-resolved or endpoint outcomes, and synthesise data modalities and evaluation protocols required for trustworthy generalisation under distribution shift. Finally, we systematically map existing ML-based predictors, review hybrid and physics-informed integration strategies, and propose a research roadmap towards data-efficient, physically consistent, and uncertainty-aware models that enable robust decision-making and scalable digital twins for cooking processes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Su Y.; Li M.; Qu T.; Huang G.Q.
Title: Temporal-digital twin-network enabled Out-of-Order synchronized control for production-intralogistics considering disturbance propagation
Abstract: Dualistic production and intralogistics (DPiL) have inherently intricate spatio-temporal coupling relationships. Meanwhile, the occurrence of disturbance propagation further amplifies such complexity, aggravating operation control difficulty. This novel problem is summarized as the dualistic production and intralogistics synchronized control problem (DPiLSynC) considering disturbance propagation. Traditional production planning and control (PPC) methods overlook the impact of disturbance propagation, significantly compromising system stability. Fortunately, digital twin (DT) technology promises rapid identification of disturbances by physical-virtual interaction. The adverse effects of disturbances may diffuse across the manufacturing system, causing operational disruptions. But analyzing the spatio-temporal characteristics of disturbance propagation is challenging due to the unclear connection-interaction mechanism of multiple DT models in manufacturing systems. This paper proposes a temporal-digital twin-network (T-DT-N) enabled Out-of-Order (OoO) synchronized control approach. Firstly, the modified OoO framework with disturbance propagation analysis is designed to reconstruct the operation logic of DPiL. Secondly, T-DT-N is developed to reveal the spatio-temporal evolution patterns of disturbance propagation by introducing the temporal network to model connection-interaction relationships of DT models. Thirdly, OoO synchronized control using propagation analysis results is proposed, involving three distinct control phases, each considering multiple factors aiming to achieve resilient DPiL operation. Computation results indicate this approach achieves shorter order makespan, shopfloor throughput time, and waiting time, while decreasing the percentage tardy. Furthermore, it exhibits stability across varying queue lengths and uncertain levels, thereby validating its application in a dynamic environment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Wu W.; Xu K.; Yang X.; Zhao Q.; Mao S.; Sun D.; Wei T.; Zhang X.; Hou X.; Zhang L.; Deng D.; Yang P.; Zhao P.; Wen C.; Wu L.; Liu R.; Zhang R.; Hu Z.; Sun Z.
Title: Artificial intelligence for advanced alloy: multiscale simulation, intelligent manufacturing, high-throughput characterization, and service performance intelligent assessment
Abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping alloy research and development by extending its role from conventional data-driven property prediction to a broader set of functions embedded in physical models, manufacturing workflows, characterization pipelines, and service assessment frameworks. This review summarizes recent progress in AI-enabled alloy development across four interconnected stages: multiscale computational simulation, intelligent manufacturing, high-throughput characterization, and service-life prediction. In computational simulation, machine learning interatomic potentials, CALPHAD-assisted models, discrete dislocation dynamics, phase-field modeling, crystal plasticity finite element methods, and ICME are discussed with emphasis on simulation acceleration, closure-relation learning, parameter inversion, and multi-scale coupling. In intelligent manufacturing, applications of AI in casting, forging, additive manufacturing, rolling, heat treatment, and metallurgical refining are reviewed, highlighting multi-source sensing, physical-field reconstruction, defect detection, process optimization, and digital-twin-based control. High-throughput characterization based on SEM, EBSD, TEM/STEM, and automated microstructure quantification is further considered as a critical data-feedback layer that links processing history, microstructural descriptors, and model calibration. For service assessment, AI-assisted prediction of corrosion, fatigue, creep, and coupled damage is summarized to clarify how composition, microstructure, defects, residual stress, environment, and loading history can be integrated for lifetime prediction and reliability evaluation. Finally, key challenges are discussed, including data scarcity and heterogeneity, insufficient physical consistency, limited extrapolation reliability, weak interoperability among models and scales, and the lack of uncertainty-aware decision-making. Future perspectives are proposed toward physics-informed learning, standardized databases, autonomous laboratories, digital twins, and closed-loop alloy development systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Toward reliable physics-informed neural networks under degradation uncertainty: An implicit-volume framework for dynamic modeling of gas turbine engines
Abstract: Accurate dynamic modeling of gas turbine engines under real-operating conditions is important for digital-twin assessment and system monitoring. Traditional component-level models rely on repeated nonlinear iterations for dynamic simulation, while standard physics-informed neural networks may suffer robustness degradation when ideal physical priors are inconsistent with degradation-affected data. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes the Implicit Volume Physics-Informed Neural Network (IVP-PINN) to improve dynamic modeling reliability for gas turbine engines under degradation uncertainty. First, a statistical error-tolerance mechanism employing a divergence metric relaxes the zero-residual constraint imposed on the flow-matching relation of the non-degraded reference model, thereby accommodating degradation-induced model mismatch without relaxing the physical mass-conservation law. Second, an implicit-volumetric architecture considering unsteady wave coupling utilizes neural network nonlinear mapping to bypass traditional iterative solvers. This simultaneously substantially reduces the computational cost and preserves authentic volumetric hysteresis effects. Validations under diverse transient disturbances and actual operational data show that IVP-PINN closely captures complex trajectories. Within the validated outside-training degradation range of [−10%, −6%), 87.75% of healthy-state predictive performance was retained at −10%. Compared with PI-LSTM, PINN, and MLP, IVP-PINN reduces peak MaxAE by 58.5%, 71.2%, and 68.0%. The proposed IVP-PINN shows potential for digital-twin dynamic assessment of gas-turbine systems.
